title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Ops Playbook
author: Sofia Ramirez
content:
Overview

Purpose:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's serving runtime reference material: architecture overview, kernel scheduling guidance, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite details, release notes practice, known issues and mitigations, and day-2 runbooks. It is intended for runtime engineers, SREs, and platform owners who operate and evolve the inference runtime.

Scope:
- GPU-backed model serving (hosted and dedicated)
- Inference runtime components: request router, scheduler, execution kernels, KV cache, batching service, and telemetry agents
- Operational procedures for profiling, benchmarking, release validation, and incident playbooks

Owners and Contacts:
- Runtime product owner: Marcus Lee (runtime-product-owner@redwood.example)
- Primary on-call: eng-serving-runtime team
- Secondary support: eng-sre

1) Runtime Architecture Summary

Intro:
The serving runtime is a modular, GPU-optimized inference engine built to deliver predictable latency and throughput across model families. Key design goals: isolation of model processes, efficient kernel execution, intelligent batching, KV cache reuse, and transparent observability.

High-level components:
- Request Router: authentication, routing policy (latency/cost/region), and request shaping.
- Work Queues and Batching Service: groups requests by model, quantization profile, and sequence-length buckets; continuous batching with time and size windows.
- Scheduler / Kernel Selection: maps micro-batches to GPU kernels, picks attention/triton kernels by shape, and triggers fallback paths.
- Runtime Execution Engine: attention kernels, rotary/ALiBi support, KV cache, and tensor memory management.
- KV Cache Store: per-session prefix caching with LRU eviction and refetch policies.
- Telemetry & Tracing Agent: token-level latency, kernel-level counters, and distributed traces.

SLOs and thresholds (example):
- P50 token latency: 10ms (short requests)
- P95 token latency: 50ms
- Outlier request rate: <=0.2%
- Availability: 99.95% for dedicated, 99.9% hosted

Ownership and boundaries:
- Scheduling and kernel tuning: serving-runtime team
- Autoscaling, infra: eng-platform and eng-sre
- Deployment and rollout policies: eng-platform with product approval

2) Kernel Scheduling Guidance

Scheduling goals:
- Maximize GPU utilization while preserving latency SLOs
- Avoid head-of-line blocking between latency-sensitive and bulk workloads

Key concepts:
- Micro-batching: break client request batches into micro-batches aligned with kernel-friendly shapes (e.g., batch sizes 1,2,4,8 depending on model).
- Shape-aware kernel selection: prefer kernels optimized for sequence-length and head-size. If custom kernel yields >15% perf improvement, mark as preferred in kernel-catalog.
- Priority lanes: 3 lanes - realtime (low-latency), mixed, batch (throughput-oriented). Realtime preempts mixed/batch within configured fair-share limits.

Config knobs (example YAML excerpt):
```yaml
scheduling:
  lanes:
    - name: realtime
      preemptible: true
      max_queue_ms: 15
    - name: mixed
      preemptible: true
      max_queue_ms: 50
    - name: batch
      preemptible: false
      max_queue_ms: 200
kernel_selection:
  prefer_custom_kernels: true
  custom_kernel_threshold_pct: 15
```

Best practices:
- Start with three-lane scheduler for mixed workloads.
- Use telemetry to identify shape distributions and update sequence-length buckets weekly.
- Maintain a kernel compatibility matrix mapping model variants to GPU families.

3) Profiling Playbook

When to profile:
- Before onboarding a new model to production
- After significant kernel / scheduler change
- When P95 latency regresses beyond release baseline

Profiling tools and instrumentation:
- Perf traces: token-level spans via our tracing agent (x-request-id correlated)
- Kernel telemetry: per-kernel execution time, SM occupancy, memory throughput (collected by nvprof/nvtx or nvidia-smi integrated exporters)
- Heap & memory: allocator fragmentation, peak GPU memory per process

Step-by-step profiling procedure:
1) Reproduce at scale in staging with representative traffic pattern. Use replay harness in /bench/replay.
2) Collect a 5-minute token-level trace and a concurrent 30s kernel-sampler run.
3) Aggregate traces, annotate slow requests, and map to kernel hot-spots.
4) If kernel contention observed, evaluate micro-batch reshaping or kernel substitution.
5) Run end-to-end latencies post-tuning and compare to baseline.

Common checks and thresholds:
- Kernel 95th percentile time should be <= 1.4x baseline for same model/shape.
- SM occupancy below 40% suggests kernel underutilization; evaluate batch packing.
- Sustained GPU memory alloc/free churn > 100 ops/s indicates allocation hotspot; enable pooled allocator.

4) Benchmarking Suite and Process

Purpose:
Standardized benchmarks to measure cost/throughput/latency across hardware, quantization profiles, and scheduling configurations. Benchmarks feed the model catalog performance profiles.

Metrics collected:
- Tokens/sec (throughput)
- P50/P95/P99 token latency
- GPU utilization (SM occupancy)
- Memory footprint (MB)
- Cost-estimated tokens/unit (based on infra pricing)

Benchmark types:
- Microbench: single-model kernel-level runs to validate kernel improvements.
- Macrobench: multi-tenant workload replay with real route mixes.
- Stress test: saturate batch lane to validate autoscaling and graceful degradation.

Benchmark cadence and ownership:
- Model onboarding: run microbench + macrobench; owning eng must provide baseline.
- Quarterly performance sweep across fleet by eng-serving-runtime + eng-sre.

Sample benchmark command:
```bash
# run macrobench in staging
./bench/run_macrobench --config benchmarks/configs/codex-mix.yaml --duration 10m --trace-out /tmp/trace.json
```

Result reporting:
- Bench results are published to the performance dashboard and attached to model catalog entries. Include commit, kernel version, and hardware SKU.

5) Release Notes and Validation Checklist

Release scope:
- Kernel upgrades, scheduler changes, new quantization profiles, runtime config changes, and agent telemetry updates.

Pre-release checklist:
1) Unit + integration tests green for runtime and kernels.
2) Microbench shows no regression >5% vs baseline for targeted shapes.
3) End-to-end macrobench in staging demonstrates P95 within SLO or has documented rollback plan.
4) Migration plan and rollback steps in PR description.
5) Update model-catalog performance profiles if behavior changes.

Release notes format (for each release):
- Summary: one-line explanation
- Impact: components and customers affected
- Benchmark delta: tokens/sec and P95 changes by model family
- Rollout plan: percentage staged rollout schedule and monitoring windows
- Rollback steps and known side effects

6) Known Issues, Workarounds, and Long-term Fixes

Active known issues (living list):
- Issue: KV cache thundering effect under high fan-out sessions
  - Symptom: burst of cold-cache requests cause P95 spikes
  - Workaround: enable per-route cache warmup and increase cache hotness threshold
  - Long-term: implement hierarchical prefetche r and per-GPU warm caches (Q3 2027)

- Issue: Custom kernel fallback on Ampere shows higher memory usage
  - Symptom: OOMs in mixed-tenant nodes during stress tests
  - Workaround: pin heavy models to dedicated nodes or use mixed precision profile
  - Long-term: memory footprint optimizations in kernel and allocator refactor

- Issue: Scheduler starvation when large batch workloads flood mixed lane
  - Symptom: realtime lane P95 increases for short bursts
  - Workaround: reduce max_queue_ms for batch lane and enable realtime preemption
  - Long-term: implement dynamic admission controller (in design)

7) Runtime Runbooks and Incident Playbooks

Critical incident triage (short version):
1) Detect: alert on P95 token latency crossing threshold and increased 5xx rate.
2) Triage: collect traces, recent deploys, kernel version, and staging benchmark results.
3) Mitigate: route realtime traffic to reserved pool or degrade to smaller model variant; scale up dedicated pool.
4) Remediate: roll back offending change or apply emergency kernel config patch.
5) Postmortem: publish within 72 hours with RCA and action items.

Runbook examples (commands):
- Collect traces for last 10 minutes:
```bash
curl -s "https://obs-api/trace?service=serving-runtime&from=-10m" -o /tmp/trace.json
```
- Force route to fallback model during incident:
```bash
redwoodctl route update --route-id r123 --fallback-model small-gptq-8bit
```
- Scale dedicated pool by adding nodes:
```bash
infra-cli scale pool serving-dedicated-pool --add 3 --region us-west-2
```
